title: 22. Interview: Horizontal Scaling
summary: Interview Q&A for Horizontal Scaling — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Horizontal Scaling interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is horizontal scaling and how does it differ from vertical scaling?
**Answer:** Horizontal scaling ("scaling out") adds more machines to a pool to share load, while vertical scaling ("scaling up", Topic 12) makes a single machine bigger. Horizontal scaling trades operational simplicity for elasticity and fault tolerance: you can survive single-node failures, autoscale with demand, and grow beyond the largest available instance type. The catch is that stateful services need sharding and replication, and distributed-systems trade-offs (CAP, PACELC) appear. Stateless services scale out trivially — any instance can serve any request — which is why modern web architectures externalize state into caches (Redis) and databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB) so that the application tier can scale horizontally without coordination.
**Visual:**
```
Vertical:  1 box  -> bigger box (96 vCPU, 768 GB)
Horizontal: 1 box -> 4 boxes -> 40 boxes (4 vCPU each, autoscaled)
```

### Q2. Why is consistent hashing preferred over naive modulo hashing for distributing keys across nodes?
**Answer:** Naive modulo hashing maps a key to node `hash(key) % N`. When N changes (a node is added or removed), nearly every key remaps to a different node — catastrophic for a database that must physically relocate data. Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a virtual ring; a key maps to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node only affects keys in that node's arc of the ring — approximately `1/N` of the keyspace. Cassandra uses this with virtual nodes (typically 256 vnodes per physical node) to spread each node's load across many ring positions, which improves balance and reduces the impact of a single node's departure. The result: cluster expansion becomes a gradual rebalance rather than a full data shuffle.
**Visual:**
```
Naive mod-3 -> mod-2: ~67% of keys move
Consistent ring add node: ~33% of keys move (1/N)
```

### Q3. What is a shared-nothing architecture and why is it important for horizontal scalability?
**Answer:** In a shared-nothing architecture, each node owns its own CPU, memory, and disk; there is no shared storage or contention point. Adding a node adds a full unit of independent capacity, so throughput scales nearly linearly. By contrast, shared-disk architectures (a SAN or cluster filesystem behind many compute nodes) eventually bottleneck on the storage controller's bandwidth and lock manager, so adding compute stops helping. Cassandra, DynamoDB, ScyllaDB, and sharded MongoDB are all shared-nothing: each shard owns its disks and serves its data locally. This is also why running Postgres with a shared NFS volume for "horizontal scale" is an anti-pattern — the storage layer becomes the bottleneck even though compute scales.
**Visual:**
```
Shared-nothing:  Node1[disk1]  Node2[disk2]  Node3[disk3]   (linear)
Shared-disk:     Node1 --> +-----------+ <-- Node3
                 Node2 --> | shared SAN |             (bottleneck)
                           +-----------+
```

### Q4. How do stateless and stateful services differ in their ability to scale horizontally?
**Answer:** Stateless services scale out trivially — any instance can serve any request because nothing is remembered between calls. You add instances behind a load balancer and traffic spreads automatically. Stateful services (databases, caches, session stores) own data, so adding a node requires partitioning (sharding) the dataset, replicating shards to the new node, and rebalancing. The new node cannot serve traffic for data it does not yet hold. This is why engineers externalize state: move sessions from local memory into Redis, move file uploads into S3, move in-process caches into Memcached. Once the application tier is stateless, it can scale from 4 to 400 instances with no code change — Kubernetes just bumps the `replicas` count.
**Visual:**
```
Stateless:   LB --> [app][app][app][app]  (add freely)
Stateful:    LB --> [db:shardA][db:shardB] + new node must REBALANCE first
```

### Q5. What is a hot shard and how do you mitigate it?
**Answer:** A hot shard is a single partition that receives disproportionate traffic — for example, sharding tweets by username when one celebrity's account generates millions of reads while others generate dozens. The overloaded node saturates while others sit idle, defeating the purpose of horizontal scaling. Mitigations include: (1) **virtual nodes** (Cassandra vnodes) so each physical node owns many small ring positions and load is statistically evened out; (2) **power-of-two-choices** — instead of always picking the least-loaded shard, pick two random candidates and choose the less loaded, which reduces queueing time dramatically; (3) **shard splitting** — break a hot shard into sub-shards (common in DynamoDB and Vitess); (4) **caching layer** (Redis) in front of the hot key. Instagram uses power-of-two-choices in their feed backend for exactly this reason.
**Visual:**
```
Bad:   shard[celeb] = 1M req/s   shard[others] = 10 req/s
Fix:   split celeb into 10 sub-shards, OR cache celebrity feed in Redis
```

### Q6. What role does the load balancer play in a horizontally scaled system?
**Answer:** The load balancer is the entry point that distributes incoming traffic across backend instances. At Layer 4 (TCP) it routes by connection — fast but opaque to the protocol. At Layer 7 (HTTP) it can route by URL path, header, cookie, or geographic origin, enabling canary releases, A/B tests, and sticky sessions. For stateful backends, the LB often uses consistent hashing on a request key so the same user always lands on the same backend that holds their cached data. Modern service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) move LB logic to a client-side proxy in each Pod, enabling locality-aware routing (prefer same-AZ backends to cut cross-AZ data-transfer cost) and retries with circuit breaking. Without a LB, horizontal scaling would require clients to know about every backend, which is unworkable at scale.
**Visual:**
```
Users --> ALB (L7) --> [path /api/*]   -> api-pool
                  --> [path /static/*] -> cdn-pool
                  --> [cookie canary]  -> canary-pool (5%)
```

### Q7. What are the main costs and trade-offs of horizontal scaling?
**Answer:** First, operational complexity: 100 instances mean 100 places for failures, 100 OS patches, 100 logs to aggregate. Netflix built the entire Simian Army to manage this. Second, distributed-systems pathologies appear: CAP and PACELC trade-offs, network partitions, clock skew, split-brain. Third, cost per unit of compute is higher — 100 `m5.large` instances cost roughly the same as one `m5.24xlarge` but deliver less raw CPU due to per-instance overhead; the savings come from elasticity (release instances off-peak). Fourth, debugging is harder — a request touching 12 microservices across 4 AZs requires distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin) to follow. The right answer is almost always: vertical-scale until you can't, then horizontal-scale out, and design for horizontal scaling from day one.
**Visual:**
```
Vertical: simple, SPOF, hardware ceiling, ACID preserved
Horizontal: complex, fault-tolerant, elastic, CAP/PACELC apply
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your stateless API service runs on 4 EC2 instances behind an ALB. Traffic doubles next quarter. Walk me through how you'd scale horizontally.
**Answer:** First, confirm the service is truly stateless — no local session storage, no in-process caches that depend on the instance. Then set up autoscaling: define a launch template with the current AMI, an autoscaling group with min=4, desired=8, max=20, and a target-tracking policy on CPU (e.g., maintain 50% average). The ALB's target group health checks ensure new instances only receive traffic once they pass. Capacity-test the new ceiling with k6 or Locust (Topic 14) before peak. Verify downstream dependencies can absorb 2× — database connection pool size, Redis maxclients, third-party API rate limits. Watch for cross-AZ data-transfer cost spikes if the new instances distribute unevenly. Finally, set an SLO (Topic 15) and a CloudWatch alarm on 5xx error rate so the autoscaler can react if a bad deploy makes the new instances unhealthy.
**Visual:**
```
ALB --> ASG(min=4,des=8,max=20) --> [i1][i2][i3][i4][i5][i6][i7][i8]
       ^                                  |
       +-- CPU target 50% (scale out) ----+
```

### Q2. You're running Cassandra with 12 nodes. The team wants to add 4 more nodes to handle a 30% traffic increase. How do you do it without downtime?
**Answer:** Cassandra supports online cluster expansion. First, set `num_tokens` to match existing nodes (typically 256 vnodes). Add nodes one at a time with `auto_bootstrap: true` — each new node joins the ring, claims token ranges from existing nodes, and streams its assigned data in the background. During streaming, existing nodes continue serving reads and writes; the new node marks itself as `UN` (up/normal) only when it has finished bootstrapping. Use `nodetool cleanup` on existing nodes afterward to remove data they no longer own. Watch streaming progress with `nodetool netstats` and compaction backlog with `nodetool compactionstats`. Add nodes sequentially, not in parallel, to avoid overwhelming the network. After expansion, run a repair to ensure replicas are in sync. This process typically takes hours-to-days for terabyte-scale clusters but incurs zero downtime.
**Visual:**
```
Before:  N1 N2 N3 ... N12  (each owns 1/12 of ring)
After:   N1 N2 ... N12 N13 N14 N15 N16  (each owns 1/16)
         New nodes streamed their ranges from existing replicas
```

### Q3. A celebrity with 50M followers posts on your platform. The "fetch this user's feed" shard saturates. How do you handle this hot key?
**Answer:** First, cache aggressively — put the celebrity's feed in Redis with a short TTL (e.g., 5 seconds); 99% of reads hit the cache, sparing the database. Second, use **read replicas** specifically for hot keys — DynamoDB and Cassandra let you increase replication factor on hot partitions or use "adaptive capacity" to dedicate more throughput. Third, **scatter-gather**: instead of one query for the full feed, fan out to per-source shards and merge — the celebrity's posts live in a "celebrity shard" that's replicated 10× while normal users live in standard shards. Fourth, **precompute** the celebrity's feed at write time (fan-out on write) so reads are O(1). This is exactly the dual-write pattern Instagram uses: famous accounts use fan-out-on-write; normal accounts use fan-out-on-read. Finally, monitor the shard's queue depth and circuit-break if it saturates.
**Visual:**
```
Bad:    GET /feed/celeb --> shard[C]  (1 node dies)
Better: GET /feed/celeb --> Redis (hit 99%) 
                          --> scatter to 10 replicas of shard[C]
                          --> precomputed fan-out write cache
```

### Q4. You sharded your Postgres database by `user_id % 16`. One shard is at 90% CPU while others are at 20%. How do you rebalance?
**Answer:** The problem is uneven distribution — some users generate 100× more traffic than others, and mod-16 hashing doesn't account for that. First, identify the heavy users via query logs and aggregate their traffic. Then implement **directory-based sharding**: maintain a lookup table mapping each `user_id` to a shard, so heavy users can be migrated individually to dedicated shards. Migrate a heavy user by: (a) dual-writing new data to both old and new shards; (b) backfilling historical data; (c) cutting reads over once backfill completes; (d) stopping writes to the old shard. Tools like Vitess, Citus, and Instagram's custom sharding layer automate this. Going forward, use a smarter shard assignment algorithm: power-of-two-choices or consistent hashing with vnodes. Monitor shard CPU variance and set an alert if any shard exceeds 1.5× the average.
**Visual:**
```
Before: shard0[user_1... celeb_user_42]  -> 90% CPU
        shard1[users]                    -> 20% CPU
        ...
After:  celeb_user_42 moved to dedicated shard16
        (via directory lookup table, dual-write migration)
```

### Q5. Your microservices architecture has 50 services, each scaling horizontally. Cross-AZ data transfer cost is exploding. What do you do?
**Answer:** Cross-AZ traffic in AWS costs ~$0.01/GB each way — at scale, this dwarfs compute cost. First, instrument with VPC Flow Logs to identify the top talkers. Likely fixes: (1) **locality-aware routing** — configure Istio/Linkerd or your service mesh to prefer same-AZ backends when available (Envoy supports this natively via `locality_weighted_balancing`); (2) **co-locate dependent services** — deploy services that call each other frequently in the same AZ using pod anti-affinity rules or topology spread constraints; (3) **batch and cache** — many cross-AZ calls are repeated lookups; cache them in a local Redis or in-memory LRU to avoid the call entirely; (4) **consolidate small services** — if `auth` and `user` always call each other, merging them eliminates the cross-AZ hop; (5) **use Availability Zone–aware LB** — AWS ALB already prefers same-AZ targets but you can verify with access logs. Re-measure monthly; a typical microservices platform can cut cross-AZ cost 60-80% with these techniques.
**Visual:**
```
Before: svcA[us-east-1a] --> svcB[us-east-1b]  ($$$ cross-AZ)
After:  svcA[1a] --> svcB[1a]  (same-AZ preferred, free)
        svcA[1b] --> svcB[1b]
```

### Q6. You're designing a multi-region active-active deployment. How does horizontal scaling interact with cross-region replication?
**Answer:** Multi-region active-active means every region accepts writes, which conflicts with single-source-of-truth models. Horizontal scaling within a region is unchanged (stateless tier behind a regional LB), but the data tier must use a multi-master or CRDT-based store. DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra (with `LOCAL_QUORUM` reads), and CockroachDB all support this. Writes propagate asynchronously between regions, so you must handle **conflict resolution**: last-write-wins (using HLCs or TrueTime), CRDTs (for counters and sets), or application-level merge. Trade-offs: read latency drops for global users (they hit a local region), but write latency increases (each write must replicate to other regions), and consistency weakens to eventual. Cross-region bandwidth is expensive, so replicate only the data each region needs, and consider topology-aware replication (e.g., EU users' data stays in EU for GDPR). Netflix runs active-active across three AWS regions precisely for this.
**Visual:**
```
        Region US (active)         Region EU (active)
        +----------------+         +----------------+
        | LB->apps->DB   | <--->   | LB->apps->DB   |
        +----------------+ async   +----------------+
                ^                              ^
                |   async replication (RPO ~1s) |
                v                              v
        Users in Americas           Users in Europe
```

### Q7. Your autoscaler adds capacity during traffic spikes, but the new instances take 5 minutes to bootstrap (JVM warmup + cache fill). How do you avoid latency spikes during the gap?
**Answer:** Five-minute cold starts violate most latency SLOs (Topic 15). Mitigations in order of preference: (1) **predictive autoscaling** — use historical traffic patterns (e.g., AWS Auto Scaling Plans, KEDA, or a custom model) to scale out 10 minutes *before* the predicted spike; (2) **over-provisioned baseline** — keep 20% extra capacity always warm, accepting the cost as the price of low latency; (3) **pre-warmed pool** — keep a small set of "spare" instances already booted and connected to the database, registered to the LB but receiving no traffic until needed; (4) **lighter runtime** — switch from JVM to GraalVM native image or Go to drop startup from minutes to seconds; (5) **staggered deploy** — for known events (Prime Day, Super Bowl), pre-scale to expected peak manually rather than relying on reactive autoscaling. Netflix uses all five: predictive scaling for daily peaks, manual pre-scale for big releases, and native-image microservices for fast elastic scaling.
**Visual:**
```
Reactive:     spike -> alarm (1m) -> provision (5m) -> warm -> serve  [SLO violated]
Predictive:   forecast -> scale 10m early -> warm by spike -> serve   [SLO held]
```
